extracted.intended_audience: science communication researchers, university press officers, and health/journalism professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for drafting press releases about genetic or mechanistic findings that preserve fidelity to the source science while remaining pickup‑worthy for lay press. Focuses on avoiding deterministic simplifications and providing appropriate contextual detail (effect sizes, population, translational and replication status, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-determinism markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release explicitly use 'associated with' / 'increased risk of' rather than 'causes' or 'the gene for'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid biologically deterministic language such as 'the gene for X' or statements implying single‑gene causation. Prefer phrasing that conveys association and uncertainty (e.g., 'is associated with', 'linked to an increased risk of'). Anti-pattern: headlines or lead sentences that assert causal relationships when the study only reports associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect-size context
rubrics_metrics.description: For a reported genetic association, does the release give both relative risk and absolute risk increase (e.g., 'from 4% baseline to 6% — a 50% relative increase')?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report absolute risks alongside relative effects to avoid inflating perceived impact. Provide baseline rates and translate relative percentages into concrete terms. Anti-pattern: reporting only a large-sounding relative increase without baseline context, which can mislead readers about practical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penetrance disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For mendelian-style claims, does the release state the penetrance (proportion of carriers actually developing the trait)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing high‑penetrance or single‑gene findings, report the proportion (penetrance) of variant carriers who exhibit the trait/condition. This prevents overstatement of risk for carriers. Anti-pattern: implying that carrying a variant guarantees disease without stating penetrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the population studied a single ethnicity / age cohort / sex? Does the release flag where generalisation is unjustified?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly note the characteristics of the study sample (ethnicity, age range, sex, clinical vs. population sample) and caution against broad generalisation when the study is limited. Example: if findings come from a single ethnic cohort, state that applicability to other groups is unknown. Anti-pattern: blanket claims about 'people' when the sample was restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory chain length
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release distinguish 'associated with' from 'mechanistically linked to' from 'intervening in this pathway changes outcome X'? Each step is a different epistemic level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate clearly between observational associations, hypothesised mechanistic links, and demonstrated causal interventions. Label each claim with its evidentiary level to avoid conflating association with mechanism or intervention efficacy. Anti-pattern: collapsing levels and implying interventions will produce the observed outcome without experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translational status
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the finding bench science, animal model, or human clinical? Does the release state which?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether results are in vitro, animal, early-phase human, or observational human research. Indicate the stage of translation and the implications for clinical relevance or immediacy. Anti-pattern: implying clinical applicability when results are preclinical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication status
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the finding been replicated in independent samples? If not, does the release say so?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether findings are novel single studies or have been replicated. If not replicated, emphasize provisional status and need for confirmation. Anti-pattern: presenting unreplicated, preliminary results as established facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deterministic-headline test
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the release's headline pass the genetics-graduate-student panel as 'non-deterministic'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an independent, informed reader (e.g., genetics graduate students) as a quick check: would they judge the headline non‑deterministic? Headlines that fail this test typically introduce deterministic simplifications that drive downstream misinterpretation. Scoring note: Brechman et al. used graduate‑student ratings of representativeness; a headline that reads as causal/definitive would count as failing.
